title: Is Broadcom Overvalued or Undervalued? Let the Numbers Decide!
subtitle: A strong business does not automatically make a good investment. A discounted cash flow model puts a number on what Broadcom could be worth.
summary: Broadcom has become one of the key players behind the AI boom. I built a DCF model to look beyond the headlines and ask what the business could actually be worth: an implied US$421.52 per share.
content:
Broadcom has become one of the key players behind the AI boom. But with so much optimism surrounding artificial intelligence, I wanted to look beyond the headlines and ask a more important question: what could the business actually be worth?

Looking Beyond the AI Hype

We have established a positive outlook from taking a look at the financial statements. Broadcom is a strong company, accelerating its growth rapidly.

But a strong business does not automatically make a stock a good investment. Even an exceptional company can be a poor investment if its share price is already pricing in future growth.

Therefore, in addition to the analysis of financial statements, I also built a discounted cash flow (DCF) model to estimate what Broadcom’s future cash-generating ability could be worth today.

Discounted Cash Flow

A DCF valuation is a method of estimating what a business is worth by finding the present value of future cash flows. The idea being that money received in the future is worth less than money received today, so future cash flow must be discounted using an appropriate rate.

I started by establishing Broadcom’s FY2026 revenue base at approximately US$105.9 billion, using reported revenue for the first nine months and management’s guidance for the fourth quarter. From there, I forecast revenue over the following ten years until FY2036. This was where the first major judgement call came in: how much of Broadcom’s AI momentum can realistically continue?

For this case, I assumed revenue growth of 60% in FY2027, followed by 35% in FY2028 and 22% in FY2029. I then gradually reduced growth to 15% in FY2030 and 4% by FY2036. I chose this declining growth trajectory because I believe Broadcom can continue benefiting from AI-related demand in the near term, while recognising that sustaining exceptionally high growth becomes increasingly difficult as a company grows larger.

Growth Is Only Half the Story

Revenue growth can make a company look impressive on paper, but I wanted to really understand how much of that growth could translate into actual cash generation.

To do this, I forecasted Broadcom’s operating margins alongside its revenue. I used management’s fourth-quarter FY2026 operating margin guidance of approximately 66% as a reference point, then assumed a gradual decline from 65% in FY2027 to 60% by FY2031, holding the margin at that level thereafter.

However, you may ask: Why not assume margins keep expanding?

My reasoning is that Broadcom’s business mix may change as AI infrastructure becomes a larger part of its operations. While AI semiconductors and networking products can be highly profitable, a greater contribution from complete AI systems and rack-level solutions could create margin pressure. Hence, my more cautious assumption.

Turning Forecasts Into Cash Flow

Once I had forecast revenue and operating profitability, I moved to the part of the DCF that matters most: unlevered free cash flow (UFCF).

I first calculated UFCF by starting with operating profit after tax, adding back depreciation and amortisation, and subtracting capital expenditure and change in net working capital. In simple terms, I wanted to estimate how much cash Broadcom could generate after paying the operating costs and making the investments needed to support its growth.

I then discounted those future cash flows using a weighted average cost of capital (WACC) of approximately 10.45%. My WACC incorporates the costs of both equity and debt, weighted with respect to Broadcom’s capital structure.

By discounting the forecast cash flows, I converted the cash Broadcom could generate in the future into an estimated present value today.

Beyond the Forecast

A company does not suddenly stop operating after ten years. At least, ideally. To account for the cash flows Broadcom could generate beyond FY2036, I used the Gordon Growth Model to estimate its terminal value.

I assumed a perpetual growth rate of 3%, representing a more mature long-term growth profile rather than an indefinite continuation of the AI boom. This produced a terminal value of approximately US$3,071,030 million at the end of the forecast period. After discounting it back to the valuation date, its present value was approximately US$1,165,327 million.

I then summed up all the present values of the forecasted cash flows, which amounted to approximately US$935,821 million.

Finally, to arrive at the enterprise value, we have to use the sum of present values of the forecasted cash flows and the present value of the terminal value. The result for enterprise value was an estimated US$2,101,149 million.

However, enterprise value is not the same as the value attributable to shareholders. I deducted net debt of approximately US$41,161 million to arrive at an estimated equity value of US$2,059,988 million. Finally, I divided that figure by approximately 4.887 billion diluted shares.

My DCF produced an implied value of US$421.52 per share.

The Final Diagnosis

That was a whole lot of numbers. And the verdict is… to be cautiously optimistic!

My valuation suggests that Broadcom could still have room to run, with an estimated intrinsic value of $421.52 per share, implying 21.7% upside from the current price of $346.25.

While Broadcom’s AI-driven growth and strong cash-generating potential make a compelling case, the valuation also depends on the company sustaining ambitious growth and maintaining resilient margins. If those expectations fall short, this could result in a very different picture.

Ultimately, I see potential in Broadcom, but always remember: even a promising business is only as attractive as the price YOU pay for it.
